claims.text: The target material is disordered, near-equimolar HfNbTaTiZr.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen represents a realistic defect or contamination level in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework couples DFT-based anharmonic phonon calculations to machine-learning-refined interatomic potentials.
The proposed framework includes a separate electron-transport model to decouple lattice and electronic thermal conduction.
The framework can independently predict the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be within ±20% of experimental total thermal conductivity over 300–1200 K.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder and oxygen-induced distortions modify local vibrational modes and phonon-scattering mechanisms.
Explicitly treating anharmonic phonon scattering, electron-phonon coupling, and realistic defects permits lattice transport to be separated from electronic transport.
Machine-learning-optimized interatomic potentials refine the interatomic interactions and scattering parameters relevant to heat transport.
Earlier Debye-based or defect-free DFT approaches typically deviate from experiment by more than 20%.
Earlier approaches conflate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
The model is applicable to ideal and oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
Additional impurities or more extreme conditions may lie outside the model's scope.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality of the machine-learning potentials and DFT anharmonic corrections.
Accurate decoupling of electron-phonon interactions is particularly uncertain at low temperatures.
A decisive test compares minimally defective HfNbTaTiZr with material intentionally containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Electrical conductivity and Seebeck measurements can be used to derive the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
The hypothesis is falsified if predicted lattice conductivity differs by more than ±20% from experimentally isolated lattice conductivity over 300–1200 K.
The hypothesis is falsified if measurements below 200 K do not show comparable lattice and electronic contributions.

contradictions.description: The main prediction benchmarks lattice-only conductivity against experimental total conductivity, whereas the falsification rule benchmarks it against the experimentally isolated lattice component. These are different quantities, especially because the hypothesis also says the electronic contribution can be comparable.
The hypothesis criticizes prior work for conflating lattice and electronic transport, yet its own stated ±20% accuracy target directly compares lattice-only predictions with total conductivity.
